title: A proof a stranger can check
objectives: Write a proof another reader can check line by line, with every step justified.

screens.title: Two write-ups
screens.prose: Two students prove that odd plus odd is even. Imagine you are a stranger checking each line.

rows: $j + k + 1$ is an integer, so $a + b$ is even. $\blacksquare$
We want $a + b = 2m$, so assume $a + b = 2m$.
Clearly this works for all odd numbers. $\blacksquare$

state.caption: Two write-ups of: the sum of two odd numbers is even

screens.question: Tap every line of write-up B that a stranger could not check.

hints.text: Line by line, ask: does it follow from what came before, with a reason?
Line 1 assumes what is to be proved. Line 2 uses one $k$ twice.
Lines 1, 2, 4 and 5 fail. Only line 3 is checkable algebra.

feedback.correct: Right. Lines 1, 2, 4 and 5 cannot be checked; line 3 can.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each line, ask whether a reader could verify it from earlier lines.

byKey.r2: Line 3 is sound algebra: a stranger can check $4k + 2 = 2(2k + 1)$.
byKey.r0: Line 1 assumes the conclusion, $a + b = 2m$. A proof may not start from what it wants.
byKey.r1: Line 2 uses one $k$ for both numbers, so it covers only $a = b$.
byKey.r3: Line 4 says "clearly" about $m$, a letter that was never properly introduced.
byKey.r4: Line 5 claims every odd pair, but the proof covered only $a = b$.

explain.text: B assumes its conclusion, uses one $k$ for two numbers, and hides gaps behind "clearly". Only line 3 can be checked. A runs forwards from the hypothesis with a reason on each line.

screens.title: What A does right
screens.prose: Write-up A can be checked line by line by someone who has never seen the problem.

rows: $j + k + 1$ is an integer, so $a + b$ is even. $\blacksquare$
We want $a + b = 2m$, so assume $a + b = 2m$.
Clearly this works for all odd numbers. $\blacksquare$

state.caption: Two write-ups of: the sum of two odd numbers is even

screens.question: Which must a proof a stranger can check contain? Select all that apply.

options.text: A statement of the claim being proved
The method, such as "we prove the contrapositive"
Every letter introduced, as in "let $n$ be an integer"
One step per line, each with its reason
The word "clearly" wherever a step is obvious
options.why: You kept "clearly". It tells the reader to stop checking, which is the opposite of the aim.

options.text: A few examples showing the claim works
options.why: You added examples. They are evidence, and a proof does not need them.

hints.text: Look at what A has in every line.
A introduces $a$, $b$, $j$ and $k$ before using them.
Claim, method, letters, reasons. No "clearly", no examples.

feedback.correct: Right. Claim, method, letters and a reason per line, ending with $\blacksquare$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what lets a reader check each line alone.

explain.text: A reader checks a proof one line at a time, so each line needs its reason. Every letter must be introduced before it is used. "Clearly" and examples give the reader nothing to check.

screens.title: Scratch work and the proof
screens.prose: Proofs are often found backwards from the goal, as in this scratch work. The written proof runs forwards, from a fact everyone accepts.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $a, b \ge 0$. A square is never negative, so $(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})^2 \ge 0$.
Start from $\tfrac{a + b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}$ and simplify until something true appears.
lines.why: You copied the scratch direction. A written proof must not start from the goal.

hints.text: The last line of the scratch work is the first line of the proof.
Then run the scratch work upwards.
Square; expand; add $2\sqrt{ab}$; divide by 2.

feedback.correct: Right. The scratch work, reversed, with a reason on each line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the true fact at the bottom of the scratch work.

byKey.d1: You kept the line that starts from the goal. That is scratch work, not proof.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: The scratch work showed which fact is enough. The proof starts there and moves forwards. Each step is one a reader can check alone.

screens.title: A missing case
screens.prose: A proof by cases must cover every case. This draft looks finished.

rows: Claim: $n^2 + n$ is even for every integer $n$.
Then $n^2 + n = 2(2k^2 + k)$, which is even.

screens.question: What must be added?

options.why: 0 is even, $0 = 2 \times 0$, so the even case already covers it.
Negative even numbers are $2k$ with $k < 0$, already covered. Negative odd numbers are not.

options.text: Nothing: the even case is the hard one.
options.why: You ranked the cases. Odd integers are not of the form $2k$, so they are unproved.

hints.text: Which integers can be written $2k$?
Odd integers cannot.
Add the case $n = 2k + 1$.

feedback.correct: Right. The odd case is missing, and without it half the integers are unproved.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the integers the draft never covers.

explain.text: The draft proves the claim for even $n$ only. Every integer is even or odd, so the odd case completes it. A stranger checking the cases would spot the gap at once.

screens.title: Arbitrary or chosen
screens.prose: A "for all" claim starts with an arbitrary element. A "there exists" claim needs one chosen witness, as in For all and there exists.
screens.question: Drop the right opening into each slot. One chip is not used.

hints.text: A is a "for every" claim; B is a "there is" claim.
A needs an argument for every $x$; B needs one $x$.
A: let $x$ be arbitrary. B: take $x = 2$.

feedback.correct: Right. Arbitrary for $\forall$, a chosen witness for $\exists$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the opening to the quantifier.

byKey.check: You chose to check three values. That is evidence for A, and more than B needs.

explain.text: For A, an arbitrary $x$ means the argument covers every integer. For B, the witness $x = 2$ settles it, since $2^2 = 4$. Taking $x = 2$ for claim A would prove one case only.

screens.title: Working backwards to something true
screens.prose: This "proof" starts from the claim and reaches a true statement. The claim is plainly false.
screens.question: Tap the line that breaks.

hints.text: Which direction does each line run?
Line 2 is fine forwards: if $-2 = 2$ then $4 = 4$.
Line 4 runs it backwards: $4 = 4$ does not give $-2 = 2$.

feedback.correct: Right. Line 4 needs squaring to reverse, and it does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the line that runs a step backwards.

byKey.r1: Squaring both sides is a valid step forwards: if $-2 = 2$ then $4 = 4$. The fault is running it back.
byKey.r0: Line 1 only states the claim. The fault is in the reasoning.
byKey.r2: Line 3 is true: $4 = 4$. The fault is what is concluded from it.

explain.text: From the claim we reached something true, but that shows nothing. Line 4 needs $4 = 4 \Rightarrow -2 = 2$, and $(-2)^2 = 2^2$ although $-2 \ne 2$. A chain from the claim to a truth proves nothing unless every step reverses.

screens.title: Steps that reverse
screens.prose:
A chain from the claim to a true statement proves the claim only if every step reverses:

$$\text{claim} \iff \cdots \iff \text{true}$$

Otherwise, write the proof forwards from the true statement.
screens.question: Which step can always be run backwards?

options.why: $(-2)^2 = 2^2$ although $-2 \ne 2$. Squaring does not reverse.
$0 = 0$ always, so nothing can be recovered. It does not reverse.

options.text: Taking the absolute value of both sides
options.why: $|-3| = |3|$ although $-3 \ne 3$. It does not reverse.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the step can be undone exactly.

explain.text: Adding 3 is undone by subtracting 3, so $a = b \iff a + 3 = b + 3$. Squaring, multiplying by 0 and taking absolute values lose information. They work forwards only.

screens.title: Correct but not checkable
screens.prose: From a write-up of the $\sqrt{2}$ proof. Every line is true, but one gives a stranger no way to check it.

rows: So $p^2$ is even, since it is 2 times an integer.
Write $p = 2r$ for an integer $r$, since $p$ is even.

screens.question: Tap the line that needs a reason.

hints.text: Which line has no "since" or named result?
Line 3 goes from $p^2$ to $p$.
It needs: by Proving the contrapositive, if $p^2$ is even then $p$ is even.

feedback.correct: Right. Line 3 needs its reason: if $p^2$ is even then $p$ is even.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the step a reader cannot check from the lines above.

byKey.r1: Line 2 gives its reason: $p^2$ is 2 times an integer.
byKey.r3: Line 4 gives its reason: $p$ is even, from line 3.

explain.text: Line 3 is true, but it rests on a lemma proved earlier. Naming it, "by the contrapositive, $p^2$ even gives $p$ even", lets a stranger check it. Correct is not the same as checkable.

screens.title: Five methods
screens.prose: Each of these claims has a natural method from this level.

rows: The product of two odd numbers is odd.
If $n^2$ is odd then $n$ is odd.
"Every odd number greater than 1 is prime" is false.

screens.question: Drop the method that fits each claim into its slot.

hints.text: E refutes a claim; D is about every $n \ge 1$.
B's hypothesis is about $n^2$; C says something does not exist.
A direct, B contrapositive, C contradiction, D induction, E counterexample.

feedback.correct: Right. One claim for each method.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each claim's shape suggests.

byKey.con: B's hypothesis is about $n^2$, so turn it round: if $n$ is even then $n^2$ is even.
byKey.cdn: C says no largest integer exists. Suppose one does.
byKey.ind: D is a formula for every $n \ge 1$, built one term at a time.
byKey.cex: E refutes a "for all" claim with one case, 9.
byKey.dir: A unpacks straight from the definition of odd.

explain.text: A unpacks odd as $2k + 1$ directly; B's hypothesis is about $n^2$, so it is turned round. C assumes a largest integer $M$ and finds $M + 1$. D grows one term at a time, and E needs only the case 9.

screens.title: A risk note
screens.prose: A risk note claims: "the book of five positions cannot lose more than £10,000 in a day." Each position's daily loss is capped at £2,000. The risk committee wants a proof it can check.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $L_1, \dots, L_5$ be the five positions' daily losses, in £.
The book's loss is $L_1 + \dots + L_5$, so it is at most £10,000, as required. $\blacksquare$
Yesterday the book lost £6,200, well under £10,000.
lines.why: You gave one day's loss. It is evidence about one day, not a proof for every day.

hints.text: Introduce a letter for each loss first.
Then use the cap on each one.
Name; cap; add; conclude.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Introduce the losses, apply the cap, then add.

byKey.d1: You kept yesterday's loss. The proof must hold on every day.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the committee would need.

explain.text: Every letter is introduced and every line has its reason. Adding five inequalities in the same direction is the one real step. The committee can check each line without asking the author.

screens.title: A colleague's version
screens.prose: A colleague writes the same proof more briefly. The committee sends it back.

rows: Let $L_1, \dots, L_5$ be the daily losses, in £.
Clearly the total is at most £10,000.

screens.question: Tap the line that is not justified.

hints.text: Which line uses "clearly"?
How does the total follow from line 2?
Line 3 skips "add the five inequalities".

feedback.correct: Right. Line 3 hides the adding step behind "clearly".
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the line whose reason is missing.

byKey.r1: Line 2 gives its reason: the cap.
byKey.r3: Line 4 follows once line 3 is justified.
byKey.r0: Line 1 introduces the letters, as it should.

explain.text: Line 3 is true, but the reader must supply the step. Writing "adding the five inequalities, $L_1 + \dots + L_5 \le 10000$" fixes it. On a risk committee, an unchecked line is a line nobody signs.

ideas: State the claim and the method, introduce every letter, and give one step per line with its reason.
Find a proof backwards if it helps, but write it forwards from facts the reader accepts.
A chain from the claim to something true proves nothing unless every step reverses.
summary.trap: Correct is not the same as checkable: "so $p$ is even" needs its reason.

quiz.prose: "Claim: $3 = -3$. Taking absolute values, $|3| = |-3|$, which is true. So $3 = -3$."
quiz.question: What is wrong?

options.text: Taking absolute values does not reverse: $|a| = |b|$ does not give $a = b$.

options.why: Both are 3, so that line is true.
The last line is false. The chain runs a one-way step backwards.

options.text: The claim should be squared instead.
options.why: Squaring fails the same way: $3^2 = (-3)^2$.

feedback.correct: Right. The step from $|3| = |-3|$ back to $3 = -3$ is invalid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the step can be run backwards.

explain.text: Taking absolute values works forwards: $a = b$ gives $|a| = |b|$. It does not reverse, since $|3| = |-3|$. So reaching a true statement from the claim proves nothing.

quiz.prose: Claim: there is an integer $n$ with $n^2 = n$.
quiz.question: Which opening proves it?

options.why: An arbitrary $n$ is for a "for all" claim. Here one witness is enough.
That assumes a much stronger claim, and a false one: $2^2 \ne 2$.
A failing case cannot prove an "exists" claim.

feedback.correct: Right. One named witness proves an "exists" claim.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A "there is" claim needs one example that works.

explain.text: $n = 1$ is a witness: $1^2 = 1$. So the claim holds, and $n = 0$ would do too. An arbitrary $n$ would be the wrong tool.

quiz.prose: A write-up of the $\sqrt{2}$ proof reads: "$q^2 = 2r^2$. Clearly $q$ is even."
quiz.question: Which reason should replace "clearly"?

options.text: $q^2$ is 2 times an integer, so even; and if $q^2$ is even then $q$ is even.

options.why: That does not follow: $q^2 = 2r^2$ gives $q = \sqrt{2}\,r$, not $2r$.
Evenness of $p$ says nothing direct about $q$.
Examples are not reasons. The line must hold for every $q$ and $r$ that fit.

feedback.correct: Right. Two reasons: $q^2$ is even, then the earlier lemma.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the reason that goes from $q^2$ to $q$.

explain.text: $q^2 = 2r^2$ makes $q^2$ even by definition. The lemma from Proving the contrapositive gives $q$ even. Both steps are now checkable.

quiz.prose: Claim: $2^n \ge n + 1$ for every whole number $n \ge 1$.
quiz.question: Which method fits best?

options.why: A counterexample refutes a claim. This one is true: $2^1 = 2$, $2^2 = 4$, and so on.
There is no hypothesis about something built from $n$ to turn round.
Checking cases is evidence. It covers ten values, not all of them.

feedback.correct: Right. A claim for every $n \ge 1$ that grows step by step suits induction.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what shape the claim has.

explain.text: Base case: $2^1 = 2 \ge 2$. Step: $2^{k+1} = 2 \cdot 2^k \ge 2(k + 1) = 2k + 2 \ge k + 2$. So induction proves it for every $n \ge 1$.
